newsitem.title: USA: Ghost of Simpson trial hangs over bomb case.
newsitem.headline: Ghost of Simpson trial hangs over bomb case.

text.p: The ghost of the O.J. Simpson case -- a trial that split the nation and raised serious legal questions -- haunts the Denver courtroom where the Oklahoma City bombing trial is under way.

Day in, day out, the ex-football star's name keeps cropping up as the judge and lawyers select a jury in the trial of Gulf War veteran Timothy McVeigh, accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people.
Lawyers for both sides ask potential jurors about the sensational 1995 Simpson murder trial. Simpson was acquitted of killing his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman.
Several jurors said Simpson was guilty, some criticised Judge Lance Ito and many said media coverage was over-the-top.

In the bombing case, U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch cut short a defence lawyer's repeated questions to a juror about Simpson trial evidence on Friday, saying: "We're not trying the O.J. Simpson case."

Millions of Americans watched every twist of Simpson's trial on TV, giving many a possibly lop-sided view of the justice system. In a civil trial this year, Simpson was held responsible and ordered to pay $33.5 million to the victims' families.
As is usual in federal court, television cameras are strictly barred from the court in the bomb trial.
Questions about the Simpson case were in the 40-page questionnaire potential jurors filled out and most jurors are happy to expand on their views -- in detail.

"I think he was guilty," an engineering manager told prosecutor Beth Wilkinson on Friday when asked what he thought about Simpson. The trial "went on way too long," said the man, who like other potential jurors was identified only by a number.
Another potential juror, a man in tears, said what happened in the Simpson trial "was a mockery of the justice system" just like his being fined in a traffic accident case.
A cardiac nurse criticised the defence in the Simpson case on Thursday, saying: "I felt they brought race into the trial to get him off because the jury was predominantly black."

"They had an extensive amount of extremely convincing physical evidence but they didn't have an eyewitness," a window cleaner said. One woman, who said she didn't know about trials, kept referring to the "time line" in the bombing case, a term that became celebrated during the Simpson trial.

The attorneys seemed to be trying to find out whether the Simpson case soured potential jurors on the justice system and what evidence they found most persuasive -- factors certain to influence their decision in the bombing case.

Bomb trial lawyers make clear in their questions that some people, following the lead of some Simpson jurors who signed book deals after the trial, might want to get on the Denver jury in hopes of becoming famous.

The Simpson case and the Oklahoma City bombing trial have similarities. In both cases, defence attorneys complained that intensive media coverage of the investigation would prejudice their client's right to a fair trial.

Both cases relied on extensive physical and forensic evidence but lacked a witness placing the defendant at the crime scene. And in the Oklahoma City bomb trial, like the Simpson trial, the defence is expected to question whether crime lab evidence was contaminated.
But the bomb trial lacks the intriguing mixture of show business, sex and race that kept Americans gripped by the Simpson trial.

Matsch seems to have taken criticism of Ito's handling of the Simpson trial to heart. He has taken strict precautions to limit publicity, placing a gag order on attorneys until jury selection is over and keeping secret for now decisions on which potential jurors are excused.
"What Judge Ito did may not be what Judge Matsch will do," chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said in court.
